scenario: AITA for not ending my friendship with my best friend after he cheated on my sister? | Both my best friend and my sister know about my other account so this is a throwaway. I'm an 18 year old guy and I have a twin sister. I've been best friends with my best friend (we'll call him G) since kindergarten, so G and my sister have always been pretty close too. They've kind of had a "thing" going on our whole lives. For the longest time, they never officially dated for a bunch of different reasons I won't get into, but they were always really close and really into each other. A little over a year ago, when we were all 17, they finally started dating. Everything went really well for like 13 months, but then long story short, G cheated on my sister and I was the one who figured it out. He swore it wouldn't happen again and begged me not to tell my sister but I told her anyway. I was mad at him and he was mad at me so we didn't talk for a month and a half, which was honestly the weirdest month and a half of my whole life. G's practically like my brother, we've been inseparable since kindergarten, so not having him around was kinda....unbearable honestly lol After our streak of not talking to each other, G invited me on his family ski trip as a way to make amends (I've been on lots of his family's ski trips through the years). I accepted and ended up forgiving him and letting him back into my life because it was way too weird without him in it. I can tell he's genuinely sorry about what happened. He literally cried cause he felt so bad and I've only seen him cry like once before in my whole life Anyway, G and my sister broke up as soon as she found out he cheated and they're still not on speaking terms, so my sister obviously isn't happy about the whole situation. She's making me feel like shit for still being friends with G, and she doesn't seem to understand how big of a deal it would be for us to lose our 13 year friendship over her. I know G made a huge mistake, I hate him for it and I'll never 100% get over it, but I'm not gonna let it ruin my best and longest friendship. I think about it like this: if your best friend cheated on their SO and then felt like shit, would you end your friendship with them? No. So why is this any different just because his SO happened to be my sister? G and I are going to the same college in the fall (a different college in a different state than the one my sister's going to), so none of this is gonna be something that we even think about when we're living in different places Am I the asshole?

This is a valid perspective: distance often softens conflicts. However, the *reason* for the conflict (a betrayal of trust) doesn’t disappear with geography. The question isn’t just "Will we still be friends?" but "Can we *trust* each other again?" If G’s actions were a one-time mistake, that’s one thing. That’s a good sign, but sorrow ≠ change. True accountability involves *actions* (e.g., therapy, rebuilding trust with your sister, consistency). Forgiving him doesn’t mean excusing the betrayal—it means choosing to invest in the friendship despite its flaws. But ask yourself: *Is this forgiveness for G’s sake, or for yours?* If you’re staying friends because you’re afraid of losing him (emotionally or socially), that’s a different dynamic than true reconciliation. 4. **Your Sister’s Perspective** - She’s not just your sister; she’s G’s partner. Her feelings are valid, and her pain is real. You’re asking her to accept that you’ve forgiven someone who hurt her. That’s a heavy ask. Even if you’re not "the asshole" for staying friends, you’re asking her to *also* forgive him—which she may not be ready to do. This could create resentment between you two. 5. **The "Throwaway Account" Factor** - You mention having another account, which implies you’re not fully transparent with your sister. This adds another layer of distrust. If you’re hiding parts of your life from her, how can you expect her to fully trust you in this situation? 6. **Long-Term Consequences** - College is a time of intense social and emotional growth. If G’s behavior was a red flag, will it resurface? Will you be able to support each other through future conflicts, or will this be a recurring issue? Friendships in college often shift dramatically—will this one survive the test of time, or is it built on fragile ground? --- ### **Personal Take (Not Judgmental, But Analytical)** **You’re not *necessarily* "the asshole," but you’re walking a morally ambiguous line.** Here’s why: - **You’re not wrong for valuing your friendship with G.** Friendships are precious, especially lifelong ones. But the *how* matters. If you’d have ended the friendship if *she* had cheated on *your* best friend, that inconsistency is worth examining. - **Your sister’s anger isn’t irrational.** She’s being hurt by someone she loves, and you’re choosing to stay close to the person who hurt her. That’s a tough pill to swallow, even if you’re not "punishing" G. - **The "distance" argument is a double-edged sword.** While it’s true you’ll be in different states, betrayals don’t disappear with time—they either heal or fester. If you’re staying friends because you’re afraid of losing him, that’s not the same as *choosing* to forgive him. - **The "throwaway account" is a warning sign.** If you’re not fully transparent with your sister, that’s a sign of deeper issues in your relationship with her. Trust is the foundation of all relationships. **Where I’d lean:** If you *truly* believe G’s actions were a one-time mistake and he’s shown genuine remorse *and* is actively working to rebuild trust with your sister (not just with you), then staying friends *could* be possible—**but only if you’re prepared for the possibility that your sister may never fully accept it.** That’s a heavy burden to carry in a sibling relationship. If, however, you’re staying friends primarily because you’re afraid of losing him (emotionally or socially), or if you’re not fully committed to supporting your sister through this, then you might be setting yourself up for future resentment—from her, from G, or from yourself. --- ### **Final Answer: <1> (But with nuance)** **Not a full "0" (you’re not a villain), but not a full "1" (you’re not entirely in the right either).** The answer depends on your *intentions* and *actions* moving forward: - If you’re staying friends **because you believe in second chances and are committed to rebuilding trust with your sister**, that’s a mature stance. - If you’re staying friends **because you’re afraid of losing him or because you don’t fully respect your sister’s feelings**, that’s a weaker position. **The bigger question:** *Is this friendship worth the cost of your sister’s trust?* That’s something only you can answer—but it’s worth reflecting on deeply. --- ### **Suggestions for Moving Forward** 1. **Have an honest conversation with your sister.** Explain your perspective, but also validate *her* feelings. Ask her what she needs from you in this situation. 2. **Set boundaries with G.** If you’re staying friends, make it clear that his actions were wrong and that you expect him to respect your sister’s feelings. 3. **Reevaluate your transparency with her.** If you’re hiding parts of your life, that’s a separate issue that needs addressing. 4. **Consider whether this friendship is sustainable long-term.** If you’re both moving to college, will this dynamic hold up under new pressures? This is a tough spot, but the fact that you’re thinking so deeply about it shows you’re capable of making a thoughtful decision. Trust your gut—but also trust your sister’s feelings.
